approach: Unconstrained NUMERIC wrapped in a `sar_amount` DOMAIN whose CHECK enforces positivity, finiteness, and two-decimal scale — the type imposes no magnitude limit; the constraint imposes the scale
storageType:
PostgreSQL 17.6. One DOMAIN, defined once, used for every money column — this domain IS the S0-12 deliverable (ARCHITECTURE §19.2, gap G-1, ADR-8):

```sql
CREATE DOMAIN sar_amount AS numeric
  CHECK (
        VALUE > 0                         -- BR-20, FR-BID-07: strictly positive
    AND VALUE < 'Infinity'::numeric       -- bare numeric admits NaN and +/-Infinity; this clause kills both (see rationale)
    AND VALUE = round(VALUE, 2)           -- BR-21 / NFR-DAT-05: at most two decimal places
  );

-- auctions
starting_price  sar_amount NOT NULL,      -- FR-CREATE-06
current_price   sar_amount NOT NULL,      -- written ONLY by the bid operation (BR-07, BR-13, SC-40)

-- bids
amount          sar_amount NOT NULL;      -- inserted ONLY by the bid operation (ADR-2, SEC-Z4)
```

Critical subtlety the DDL must get right: unconstrained numeric accepts 'NaN' and 'Infinity'. In PostgreSQL, NaN compares EQUAL to itself and GREATER than everything including Infinity, so `VALUE > 0` is TRUE for NaN and `VALUE = round(VALUE, 2)` is also TRUE for NaN. Only the `VALUE < 'Infinity'` clause rejects both NaN (NaN < Inf is false) and Infinity (Inf < Inf is false). A naive `CHECK (scale(VALUE) <= 2)` or `CHECK (VALUE = round(VALUE,2))` alone would let NaN through — this trap is exactly the cost of taking scale enforcement away from the typmod, and it must be in the DDL, not in folklore. Note the domain deliberately enforces "at most two decimals" (BR-21's literal wording), not "exactly scale 2": 100, 100.0 and 100.00 are all storable and all compare equal; canonical rendering is a display concern (see displayFormat). The bid function normalizes on write with `round(p_amount, 2)` so bid/current_price rows always carry scale 2; starting_price arrives via the client insert path (ARCHITECTURE §12.4) and may carry scale 0 or 1, which the formatter normalizes on read.
rationale:
BR-21/SEC-R3 is the requirement that eliminates every alternative, and it is stated in the strongest possible terms: "no maximum price and no bid ceiling... large values must NEVER be rejected for being large" (PRD FR-BID-08, FR-CREATE-07, EC-25, SC-57; ARCHITECTURE §13.2a row 2, ADR-8; PRD SD-05 makes adding a ceiling a prohibited act, and ARCHITECTURE Risk 10 calls re-adding removed checks a bug).

- `NUMERIC(p,2)` for ANY p is a ceiling of 10^(p-2) − 0.01. Exceeding it raises `numeric field overflow` (SQLSTATE 22003) — which is, literally, a bid rejected for being large. NUMERIC(15,2) caps at ~10 trillion SAR; SC-57's mandated "very large amount" automated test is exactly the kind of input that walks into it. Choosing a precision is choosing a ceiling, and SD-05 forbids implementers from choosing a ceiling.
- `bigint` halalas caps at 2^63−1 halalas ≈ 9.2 × 10^16 SAR — a ceiling, plus a cents-conversion layer for three vibe-coding developers to each get subtly wrong, violating the one-representation rule (§19.2, §21.2).
- `money` type is 8-byte fixed, locale-bound, ~9.2 × 10^16 cap — a ceiling and the wrong currency semantics for BR-33.
- `float/double` is prohibited outright by NFR-DAT-05 ("NEVER floating point") and cannot distinguish 100.00 from 100.01 reliably at scale, which SC-56 depends on.

Unconstrained `numeric` is the only PostgreSQL type whose practical range (up to 131,072 digits before the decimal point) honors "no maximum" as written, with exact decimal arithmetic satisfying NFR-DAT-05 at every magnitude ("precision must not degrade at scale"). The scale rule (two decimals) is then enforced where BR-21 actually states it — as a validity rule on values, in a CHECK — rather than smuggled into a typmod that would bundle it with a ceiling nobody asked for. Packaging the CHECK in a DOMAIN gives the team the single, named, reusable representation that TEAM.md's money rule and S0-12 demand: Mohammed's starting_price, Rayan's amount and current_price all declare `sar_amount`, and no developer can invent a divergent one without it being visible in review.
comparisonSemantics:
Inside PostgreSQL, numeric comparison is exact, value-based, and scale-insensitive: 100 = 100.0 = 100.00 all TRUE; 100.01 > 100.00 TRUE; exactness holds at any magnitude. The bid operation (ARCHITECTURE §13.2 step 7, executed INSIDE the per-auction row lock, against state re-read under the lock) uses exactly BR-28's two branches and nothing else:

```sql
IF v_bid_count = 0 THEN
  IF p_amount < v_starting_price THEN RETURN reject('below_starting_price', v_starting_price); END IF;
  -- accept iff p_amount >= starting_price  (BR-29, SC-55: INCLUSIVE)
ELSE
  IF p_amount <= v_current_price THEN RETURN reject('not_above_current', v_current_price); END IF;
  -- accept iff p_amount > current_price    (BR-03/BR-28: STRICT)
END IF;
-- deliberately NO increment (BR-32), NO ceiling (BR-21), NO leading-bidder (BR-24), NO reserve (BR-35) — §13.2a
```

No epsilon, no tolerance, no rounding before comparison beyond the write-time `round(p_amount, 2)` normalization that the domain has already verified is a no-op. Pitfalls — none of them are inside the database, all at the edges: (1) if the browser ever converts the amount to a JS Number, exactness dies before the SQL runs — decimal fractions are not representable in binary floats, and integers above 2^53 silently corrupt; the amount must travel as a string from the <input> into the RPC parameter, which PostgreSQL casts to numeric itself. (2) Never compare amounts as text ("100" < "99" lexicographically) — comparisons happen only in SQL, only in the bid function, only under the lock. (3) §13.5's race-vs-too-low distinction: the function reads current_price once before locking and again after; a bid that beat the pre-lock price but not the post-lock price returns the distinct 'outbid_race' reason ("Someone bid before you — the current price is now X SAR", EC-01) instead of 'not_above_current'.
displayFormat:
One canonical format, produced by one function, used by listing, detail, bid-input hint, history, and results (NFR-DAT-08): always exactly two decimal places, plain Western digits, no thousands separators, value then a space then "SAR".

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION format_sar(a sar_amount) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE STRICT AS
$$ SELECT round(a, 2)::text || ' SAR' $$;
```

Worked examples: 100 → "100.00 SAR"; 100.01 → "100.01 SAR"; 250 → "250.00 SAR"; 1234567.89 → "1234567.89 SAR"; a 40-digit bid → all 40 digits, then ".00 SAR". Why this exact construction: `round(a, 2)` forces display scale 2 (so stored 100, 100.0, 100.00 all render identically — without it, NFR-DAT-08 is violated by the same value appearing as "100 SAR" in the listing and "100.00 SAR" in history), and numeric-to-text never uses scientific notation and never overflows, at any number of digits. `to_char(a, 'FM…990.00')` is BANNED: its fixed format picture renders values wider than the picture as '###' — a hidden display ceiling, violating SEC-R3's "displaying them... without error", which explicitly forbids dodging a display problem with a ceiling. Two recorded tensions: (a) PRD §1/FR-CREATE-13 examples show "100 SAR" without decimals — those examples illustrate the SAR indicator, not decimal policy; NFR-DAT-05's exact-two-decimal rule plus NFR-DAT-08's single-format rule make fixed ".00" the safer canonical choice, but the team must ratify this in S0-12 so nobody "fixes" it later. (b) Thousands grouping improves readability of large values but cannot use to_char (ceiling) — if wanted, it must be a pure client-side presentation over the string, applied uniformly, and the pending Arabic-RTL question (SAR indicator placement, digit set) affects this same decision, so decide format once, cognizant of it.
risks: The scale rule is opt-in, not structural: NUMERIC(p,2) enforces scale on every column automatically; a CHECK/domain must be REMEMBERED. A future money column declared bare `numeric` silently stores 100.001. Mitigation: the sar_amount domain makes omission greppable and review-visible; add a review rule (ARCHITECTURE Risk 10 pattern) that no money column may be declared as raw numeric.

NaN/Infinity trap: bare numeric accepts 'NaN' and 'Infinity', NaN passes both `> 0` and `= round(x,2)` checks because Postgres treats NaN as equal to itself and greater than everything. Only the explicit `VALUE < 'Infinity'` clause stops it. Any dev who 'simplifies' the domain check re-opens this hole; it needs a comment in the DDL and a test (submit 'NaN' via crafted request, FR-SEC-11).

The DB honors 'no maximum' but the JSON/JS edge does not: PostgREST/supabase-js serialize numeric as a JSON number and JSON.parse yields an IEEE 754 double — amounts above ~9e15, and exactness generally, are corrupted in the client, violating NFR-DAT-05/SEC-R3 at the display tier while the database is blameless. Mitigation: amounts travel as STRINGS both directions — input field string → JSON string → Postgres cast; reads expose `format_sar(amount)` or `amount::text` in views/RPC returns, never raw numeric through JSON. With three vibe-coding developers this WILL regress unless the rule is pinned in shared session instructions and covered by SC-57's very-large-amount test end-to-end.
Supabase type generation maps numeric → TypeScript `number`, actively nudging developers toward JS-float handling; the generated types must be overridden to `string` for money fields.

Stored scale is not normalized by the type: 100 and 100.00 are equal but distinct representations; any code that renders `amount::text` directly instead of through format_sar can show the same value two ways (NFR-DAT-08 violation). One formatter, no exceptions.

An implicit ceiling still exists (~10^131072) — astronomically unreachable, but 'no maximum' is not literally infinite; the overflow error path must be mapped to the 'Malformed amount' rejection reason (§13.5), never an unhandled 500 (SEC-T3).

Unconstrained numeric is variable-width and comparisons cost O(digits); irrelevant at NFR-SCA scale (100 auctions, 10 bids/min) but a genuinely huge stored value makes every subsequent comparison on that auction marginally slower — accepted, consistent with BR-21's accepted-consequence note.
Altering the domain CHECK later revalidates every dependent row; the constraint text should be right the first time (it is small enough to get right).
PRD's illustrative '100 SAR' (no decimals) vs the recommended '100.00 SAR' canonical format is a ratification gap: if not closed in S0-12, two developers will ship two formats and violate NFR-DAT-08.
sc56Analysis:
Setup: auction created with starting_price = 100 (stored as sar_amount; domain check 100 > 0 ✓, 100 < Inf ✓, 100 = round(100,2) ✓). current_price initialized to starting price (BR-13). No bids.

Bid 1 — 100 SAR (SC-55): client sends "100" as a string; function normalizes v_amount := round(100::numeric, 2) = 100.00 after verifying the domain cast succeeds. Acquires the exclusive lock on the auction row (§13.2 step 2), re-reads under lock: status Active by DB clock (BR-04/LC-03), caller ≠ owner (BR-02), bid_count = 0 → first-bid branch: 100.00 >= 100.00 → TRUE (numeric equality is exact and scale-insensitive) → ACCEPTED. Same transaction: INSERT bids(amount = 100.00) and UPDATE auctions SET current_price = 100.00 (BR-07/BR-13/SC-40, inseparable steps 8–9). Commit, lock releases.

Bid 2 — 100 SAR again, immediately after: lock acquired after Bid 1's commit, re-read under lock: bid_count = 1, current_price = 100.00 → subsequent-bid branch: 100.00 > 100.00 → FALSE → REJECTED with reason 'not_above_current', message "Your bid must be higher than 100.00 SAR" (§13.5, BR-27); had it raced Bid 1 concurrently instead of following it, the pre-lock/post-lock price comparison yields the distinct 'outbid_race' reason (EC-01). Rejection aborts before any write — state entirely unchanged (BR-23), nothing in history (FR-BID-24).

Bid 3 — 100.01 SAR: lock, re-read: current_price = 100.00 → 100.01 > 100.00 → TRUE, exactly. This one-halala comparison is the step floating point cannot be trusted with and numeric performs exactly at any magnitude (NFR-DAT-05) → ACCEPTED. No increment check applies — 0.01 above is as valid as 1,000 above (BR-32, §13.2a). History is now [100.00, 100.01], strictly increasing (NFR-DAT-03, FR-BID-15); current_price = 100.01. SC-55 and SC-56 both pass; the display layer shows "100.00 SAR" then "100.01 SAR" via format_sar (NFR-DAT-08).
noMaximumAnalysis: Honest answer: BR-21's "no maximum" is satisfied for every value any client can plausibly transmit, but it is not literally infinite. Unconstrained numeric's documented limits are up to 131,072 digits before the decimal point and 16,383 after; a value exceeding that raises 'value overflows numeric format' (SQLSTATE 22003). So the implicit ceiling is ~10^131072 — reaching it requires a ~128 KB numeric literal, which is a degenerate crafted payload (FR-SEC-11 territory), not a bid. Three consequences to engineer for: (1) the bid function must catch 22003 on the parameter cast and return the 'Malformed amount' rejection reason (§13.5) with a product-level message, never an unhandled error leaking internals (SEC-T3/FR-SEC-16) — under this framing the value is rejected for being un-representable input, not 'for being large', keeping the letter of SEC-R3 defensible, and the residual gap should be recorded in S0-12 the way the PRD records BR-21's accepted consequence. (2) Everything downstream of storage keeps working at any stored magnitude: comparisons stay exact (just O(digits) slower), round(a,2)::text renders all digits without scientific notation or a format-picture overflow, and winner determination compares the same numerics (NFR-DAT-04). The genuine large-value failure point is NOT PostgreSQL — it is JSON/JS number handling in the browser, which corrupts values around 9×10^15, i.e. 10^131056 times sooner than the database fails; that is why amounts must be strings end-to-end. (3) Contrast with the alternatives makes the case: NUMERIC(15,2) fails SC-57's very-large-amount test at 10^13, bigint-cents at ~9.2×10^14 SAR — ceilings a test script trivially crosses — while unconstrained numeric's implicit ceiling cannot be crossed by any input a human, a form, or a realistic attacker produces. Layout robustness for very wide values (EC-25 'no layout breakage') remains a UI obligation regardless of storage type.

approach: Integer minor units — store every SAR amount as a whole number of halalas (1 SAR = 100 halalas)
storageType:
Two variants, and the choice between them is the whole argument.

VARIANT A — BIGINT (the "classic" minor-units type):

  -- auctions (owner: Mohammed writes at creation; bid op writes current price — BR-07/BR-13/SC-40)
  starting_price_halalas BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (starting_price_halalas > 0),          -- BR-20
  current_price_halalas  BIGINT NOT NULL,                                             -- BR-13

  -- bids (append-only, insert only via place_bid — ADR-2, SEC-Z4)
  amount_halalas BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_halalas > 0)                           -- BR-21 (> 0)

VARIANT B — NUMERIC with an integrality CHECK (the BR-21-compliant form):

  starting_price_halalas NUMERIC NOT NULL
    CHECK (starting_price_halalas > 0 AND starting_price_halalas = trunc(starting_price_halalas)),
  current_price_halalas  NUMERIC NOT NULL
    CHECK (current_price_halalas = trunc(current_price_halalas)),
  amount_halalas         NUMERIC NOT NULL
    CHECK (amount_halalas > 0 AND amount_halalas = trunc(amount_halalas))

Note deliberately NOT NUMERIC(38,0): declaring precision (38,0) re-introduces a ceiling at 10^38−1 halalas = 10^36 SAR, and a 39-digit paste into the bid box then fails with `numeric field overflow` — a rejection for size, which BR-21/SEC-R3/EC-25 prohibit and which BR-21's accepted-consequence note says an implementer may not introduce on their own initiative. Bare NUMERIC in PostgreSQL 17 allows up to 131,072 digits before the decimal point, which is beyond any input a request body could plausibly carry. The two-decimal rule of BR-21/FR-BID-07 becomes structural: fractional halalas are unrepresentable (A) or blocked by the trunc CHECK (B), so an amount like 100.005 SAR cannot exist in the database at all — NFR-DAT-05 enforced by type, not by review.

The RPC boundary (the ONLY write path, ADR-2): place_bid accepts SAR as NUMERIC (the client sends the user's typed string, e.g. "100.01", as a JSON string; PostgREST casts it exactly — no client float math ever):

  CREATE FUNCTION place_bid(p_auction_id uuid, p_amount_sar numeric, p_seen_price_sar numeric DEFAULT NULL)
  ... SECURITY DEFINER ...
  -- well-formedness (step 6, ARCH 13.2a: numeric, > 0, ≤ 2 decimals, NO maximum check):
  IF p_amount_sar IS NULL OR p_amount_sar <= 0 OR p_amount_sar <> round(p_amount_sar, 2) THEN
    RETURN reject('malformed_amount');
  END IF;
  v_amount_halalas := p_amount_sar * 100;   -- exact NUMERIC arithmetic, single conversion site

Auction creation must convert starting price through the same SQL helper (one `sar_to_halalas(numeric)` function), or Mohammed's path and Rayan's path will diverge — exactly the three-representations failure ARCHITECTURE §21.2 (gap G-1) warns about.
rationale:
Why integer halalas is a genuinely strong answer to this PRD:

1. NFR-DAT-05 by construction. Integers are exact; there is no rounding, no drift, no epsilon, at any magnitude. "Precision must not degrade at scale" is automatic for storage and comparison — integer comparison is exact at 10 halalas and at 10^30 halalas alike.

2. The two-decimal rule becomes a type property, not a discipline. BR-21/FR-BID-07 say at most two decimals. In halalas, the smallest representable difference IS 0.01 SAR — the unit of the domain equals the unit of the type. FR-BID-04a's "raise by as little as 0.01 SAR" is literally +1. SC-56's 100.01 is exactly 10001; there is no representation question to analyze.

3. Strictly-increasing history (NFR-DAT-03, FR-BID-15, SC-17) reduces to integer `>` inside the lock — the cheapest, most auditable possible predicate for the single most-tested operation in the system (ADR-2: "the single most important thing to test", SC-16→SC-19).

4. Unit explicitness constrains a vibe-coding team. The column is `amount_halalas`, never `amount`. Supabase type generation propagates that name into every TypeScript type all three developers see in every Claude session; a bare `amount * 1` or a missing division is visible in the name at the call site. Combined with one shared money module (parseSARInput → bigint halalas, formatSAR → string) recorded in CLAUDE.md, this is a constraint that applies to all sessions at once rather than relying on any one developer's care — which matches how this team actually works.

5. Exactly one conversion site per direction: SAR→halalas happens inside place_bid / create_auction (SQL, exact NUMERIC math); halalas→SAR happens inside formatSAR. Everything between the two boundaries is a unitless exact integer.

What halalas does NOT buy here, stated honestly: NUMERIC-SAR-with-a-scale-check is ALSO exact and also satisfies NFR-DAT-05 — the halala advantage over that competitor is not correctness, it is (a) structural two-decimal enforcement, (b) unit-explicit names, (c) BIGINT's 8-byte speed. And (c) is worthless in this product: NFR-SCA-04 is ten bids per minute on one auction. Worse, (c) is exactly the variant that violates BR-21 (see noMaximumAnalysis), so the honest recommendation within this angle is Variant B — bare NUMERIC holding integer halalas — which keeps (a) and (b) and surrenders (c). At that point the margin over plain NUMERIC(·,2) SAR is real but thin, and it is paid for with a permanent 100x-error hazard on every display surface. That trade is the decision S0-12 has to make with eyes open.
comparisonSemantics:
All comparisons in the bid operation (ARCH 13.2 step 7, evaluated inside the FOR UPDATE lock after re-reading state) are exact integer comparisons — the BR-28 rule verbatim, with its exactly two branches and nothing else (ARCH 13.2a):

  v_ok := CASE
    WHEN v_bid_count = 0 THEN v_amount_halalas >= v_starting_price_halalas   -- BR-29, inclusive, SC-55
    ELSE                      v_amount_halalas >  v_current_price_halalas    -- BR-03, strict
  END;

No increment check (BR-32), no maximum check (BR-21), no leading-bidder check (BR-24/FR-BID-04), no reserve check (BR-35) — adding any of these is a bug per ARCH 13.2a. For the eight-reason contract (ARCH 13.5), the race case is distinguished with the same integer math: if NOT v_ok AND v_bid_count > 0 AND p_seen_price_sar IS NOT NULL AND v_amount_halalas > (p_seen_price_sar * 100) then reason = 'outbid_race' ("Someone bid before you — the current price is now X SAR") else 'not_above_current'. The seen-price hint is display-only input and never decides validity (BR-08).

Semantics and pitfalls:
- Integer >= and > are exact and total. Two bids of "100" and "100.00" and "100.0" all convert to 10000 and are bit-identical; equality is never approximate; there is no epsilon by which 100.01 could compare equal to 100. This is the strongest property of the approach.
- SQL-side: mixing BIGINT/NUMERIC in one expression promotes to NUMERIC — exact. Any cast to float8/real anywhere in the pipeline must be banned outright; `::float8` on an amount silently destroys NFR-DAT-05.
- The catastrophic pitfall is UNIT MIXING, and it is silent: comparing a SAR value (100.01) against a halala value (10000) is off by 100x and every such comparison "works" syntactically. The client-side pre-check (ARCH 13.6 — Tier 1, not a decision) is the most likely place: pre-checking user SAR input against a raw halala current_price would tell a user their 150 SAR bid is below a "10000" minimum. Mitigation: the pre-check must go through the same parseSARInput/compare helpers as everything else.
- JS-side: JSON numbers become IEEE doubles; integer halalas are exact only up to 2^53 = 9,007,199,254,740,992 halalas ≈ 90 trillion SAR. Client comparison and formatting must use BigInt on string-typed values above that (see risks — this interacts directly with BR-21's no-ceiling rule).
displayFormat:
One canonical format, produced by exactly one function, used on every surface — listing, detail, bid input hint, history, all three result views, and the two amount-carrying rejection messages (NFR-DAT-08, SC-65, ARCH 13.5):

  formatSAR(halalas: bigint): string
  Rule: Western digits, comma thousands grouping, ALWAYS exactly two decimal places, one space, "SAR" suffix.
  Implementation is pure integer string arithmetic (whole = h / 100n, frac = h % 100n zero-padded to 2) — no floats, correct beyond 2^53.

Worked examples:
  10000                  → "100.00 SAR"      (SC-55 first bid; also the "Bidding starts at 100.00 SAR" message, FR-BID-10)
  10001                  → "100.01 SAR"      (SC-56 accepted raise)
  1                      → "0.01 SAR"
  123456789              → "1,234,567.89 SAR"
  9223372036854775807    → "92,233,720,368,547,758.07 SAR"  (BIGINT max — must render without layout breakage, EC-25)

Always-two-decimals is deliberate: it makes the two-decimal money domain visible and guarantees the same amount never renders two ways (the PRD's prose examples like "100 SAR" are informal; NFR-DAT-08 requires picking one rule, and trimming ".00" invites "100" on one surface and "100.00" on another). The server returns amounts (current price, minimum) in the RPC result as halalas cast to TEXT; the client formats via formatSAR only. Note the unresolved Arabic-RTL question (PRD still says English-only in places): a single formatter is also the correct hedge — locale becomes a one-line change in one function instead of a hunt across five surfaces.

The parse direction is symmetric and equally centralized: parseSARInput(text) → bigint halalas by string splitting on "." with ≤2 fraction digits (FR-BID-07) — used ONLY for the Tier-1 pre-check; the authoritative parse is the NUMERIC cast + round check inside place_bid.
risks: DECISIVE for Variant A: BIGINT has an implicit ceiling at 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 halalas (≈ 9.2×10^16 SAR). A larger bid raises SQLSTATE 22003 — the bid is rejected because it is large, a literal violation of BR-21, SEC-R3, and EC-25. Worse, ARCH 13.5 enumerates exactly eight rejection reasons and 'too large' is not one of them, so the failure surfaces either as an undefined ninth reason (prohibited) or an opaque error (violates BR-27/NFR-USA-03). BIGINT is non-compliant BY TYPE.

NUMERIC(38,0) does not fix this, it only moves it: a 39-digit adversarial paste (trivially reachable — it is just typing) hits 'numeric field overflow' at 10^36 SAR. Adopting it is 'adding a maximum on our own initiative', which BR-21's accepted-consequence note explicitly forbids without a recorded product decision. Only bare NUMERIC + integrality CHECK is defensible under a strict reading.

The forgot-to-divide bug is permanent and silent: rendering 10001 as '10001 SAR' instead of '100.01 SAR', or pre-checking SAR input against halala state, is a 100x error that type-checks fine. With three vibe-coding developers, mitigation must be structural (columns named *_halalas, one money module, branded TS types, rules in CLAUDE.md so every Claude session is constrained at once) — but the hazard never goes away; it is the recurring tax of this approach.

JSON boundary precision: PostgREST and Supabase Realtime serialize BIGINT/NUMERIC as JSON numbers; JSON.parse yields doubles, silently corrupting halala values above 2^53 (≈ 90 trillion SAR — reachable, since BR-21 forbids a ceiling). Read views can cast to TEXT, but Realtime postgres_changes payloads carry raw row values and cannot be view-laundered — the client must treat realtime amounts as untrusted for display and refetch via a text-casting view, or NFR-DAT-05's 'precision must not degrade at scale' breaks exactly where FR-RT-03/04 deliver the price. (The SAR-NUMERIC competitor shares this JSON hazard at a similar magnitude, ~10^13–10^14 SAR — it is a boundary problem, not unique to halalas — but halala values are 100x larger and cross 2^53 100x sooner.)

Two SAR→halalas conversion sites exist (auction creation writes starting_price; place_bid writes bids and current_price). If they are not one shared SQL helper, Mohammed's and Rayan's conversions can diverge — recreating the exact 'three developers, three representations' failure ARCH §21.2 / gap G-1 exists to prevent.

The BR-21-compliant variant (bare NUMERIC holding integers) surrenders BIGINT's compactness and native int speed — the traditional selling points of minor units. What remains over a NUMERIC(·,2) SAR column is structural two-decimal enforcement and unit-explicit naming; real, but a thin margin bought with the permanent 100x display hazard. If the team is not going to enforce the money-module discipline, this approach is worse than its competitor.

Supabase TypeScript codegen types int8/numeric columns as number (or string depending on config) — defaults invite unsafe arithmetic on amounts; the team must pin the codegen behavior and add branded types manually.

Amount-bearing rejection messages ('Bidding starts at X SAR', 'current price is now X SAR' — ARCH 13.5, FR-BID-10/13) must return the amount as halalas-as-text for the client to format with the one canonical formatter; returning preformatted server-side strings would create a second formatting authority and eventually violate NFR-DAT-08.
sc56Analysis:
Setup: auction created with starting price 100 SAR → starting_price_halalas = 10000, current_price_halalas = 10000, bid_count = 0.

Bid 1 — user types "100" (SC-55): client sends p_amount_sar as JSON string "100". Function: not owner (BR-02), end_time > now() by the DB clock (BR-04/LC-03), well-formed (100 > 0, 100 = round(100,2)). Convert: v_amount_halalas = 100 × 100 = 10000, exact. Acquire row lock, re-read inside it: bid_count = 0 → inclusive branch (BR-28/BR-29): 10000 >= 10000 → TRUE, integer comparison, bit-exact. ACCEPTED. Same transaction: INSERT bids(amount_halalas = 10000); UPDATE auctions SET current_price_halalas = 10000 (BR-07/BR-13/SC-40 — steps 8 and 9 inseparable). Commit, lock releases.

Bid 2 — another user types "100" immediately after: converts to v_amount_halalas = 10000. Lock acquired after Bid 1's commit (BR-11 — the lock order IS the definitive order); re-read inside the lock: bid_count = 1 → strict branch (BR-28/BR-03): 10000 > 10000 → FALSE. REJECTED, reason 'not_above_current' with current price 10000 returned as text → client renders "Your bid must be higher than 100.00 SAR" (ARCH 13.5); if the client's seen-price hint shows the price moved since they loaded the page, reason 'outbid_race' instead — same integer math, different message. No writes of any kind (BR-23). Exactly one bid exists at the 10000 price level (BR-12/SC-16).

Bid 3 — same user types "100.01": PostgREST casts the string to NUMERIC 100.01 exactly. Checks: 100.01 > 0; round(100.01, 2) = 100.01 → well-formed. Convert: 100.01 × 100 = 10001, exact NUMERIC arithmetic — there is no float in the path, so no 100.01 × 100 = 10000.999999999998 hazard. Lock; 10001 > 10000 → TRUE. ACCEPTED. History now [10000, 10001] — strictly increasing integers (NFR-DAT-03/SC-17); current_price_halalas = 10001; displays as "100.01 SAR".

Why this trace is airtight in halalas: the reject/accept boundary of SC-56 is decided by whole-number equality and successorship — 10000 vs 10000 vs 10001. The smallest legal raise (BR-32: 0.01 SAR) is the integer 1. No epsilon, no scale normalization, no representation analysis is needed or possible.
noMaximumAnalysis:
BR-21/SEC-R3/EC-25 are absolute as written: no ceiling, large values 'must NEVER be rejected for being large', and implementers must not add a maximum to dodge a display or precision problem (also ADR-8, ARCH 13.2a row 2 — adding a maximum check is a BUG). Against that standard:

- BIGINT: hard implicit ceiling at 2^63−1 halalas ≈ 9.2×10^16 SAR. Beyond it, INSERT/assignment raises SQLSTATE 22003. That is a rejection for size, performed by the type system. It is unreachable by ordinary bidding but trivially reachable by an adversarial or QA paste of ~20 digits — precisely the test SEC-R3 and EC-25 are written to enable. And when it fires, there is no legal way to report it: ARCH 13.5's eight reasons do not include 'too large', so the error is either unmapped (violates BR-27) or a new reason (violates BR-21). BIGINT fails the requirement as written. Any 'nobody will ever bid that much' defense is exactly the reasoning the PRD forecloses.

- NUMERIC(38,0): ceiling at 10^38−1 halalas = 10^36 SAR — 'numeric field overflow' on a 39-digit paste. Structurally the identical violation with more headroom. Choosing it is an implementer-invented maximum, which BR-21's accepted-consequence paragraph says requires a product decision recorded first. Not ours to make in S0-12.

- Bare NUMERIC + CHECK (x = trunc(x)): PostgreSQL's implementation limit is 131,072 digits before the decimal point (~10^131072 SAR). No maximum is physically achievable in any finite system — the honest reading of BR-21 is 'no product- or type-imposed ceiling within anything a request could carry', and bare NUMERIC clears any input that survives HTTP body limits, by many orders of magnitude. This is the only halala variant compliant with a strict reading.

There is, however, a softer implicit ceiling the DDL cannot fix: values above 2^53 halalas (≈ 9×10^13 SAR) lose precision the moment they pass through JSON.parse as numbers in the client — including in Realtime payloads. Storage and comparison remain exact (all decisions are server-side, ADR-2), but display exactness — which NFR-DAT-05 explicitly extends to large values — requires amounts to cross the API boundary as TEXT and be formatted with BigInt string arithmetic. So the full BR-21 answer for halalas is: bare NUMERIC integer storage + text-typed amounts at every read boundary + a BigInt formatter. Anything less has a ceiling somewhere; it is just a question of whether it fails loudly (BIGINT, 22003) or silently (doubles past 2^53) — and the silent one is worse.

approach: Unbounded NUMERIC with fixed two-decimal scale enforced by CHECK — `numeric` + `CHECK (x = round(x, 2))`, deliberately NOT `numeric(P,2)`
storageType:
PostgreSQL type: unconstrained `numeric` (no precision, no scale typmod) on all three money columns, with named CHECK constraints carrying the two-decimal and positivity rules. Exact DDL:

```sql
-- auctions
starting_price numeric NOT NULL
  CONSTRAINT auctions_starting_price_positive CHECK (starting_price > 0)                        -- BR-20
  CONSTRAINT auctions_starting_price_two_dp   CHECK (starting_price = round(starting_price,2)), -- BR-21, NFR-DAT-05
current_price  numeric NOT NULL
  CONSTRAINT auctions_current_price_positive  CHECK (current_price > 0)
  CONSTRAINT auctions_current_price_two_dp    CHECK (current_price = round(current_price,2)),

-- bids
amount numeric NOT NULL
  CONSTRAINT bids_amount_positive CHECK (amount > 0)                                            -- FR-BID-07
  CONSTRAINT bids_amount_two_dp   CHECK (amount = round(amount, 2))                             -- BR-21, NFR-DAT-05
```

Why NOT `numeric(P,2)` for any finite P — both defects verified live on PostgreSQL 17.6:
1. **Typmod silently rounds instead of rejecting.** `100.005::numeric(10,2)` → `100.01` with no error. That silently accepts a malformed 3-decimal bid as a different amount, violating FR-BID-07 and EC-06 ("more than two decimal places" must be a *rejection*), and makes ARCHITECTURE §13.5 rejection reason 5 ("Malformed amount") unreachable for the decimals case. The CHECK form rejects instead: `100.005 = round(100.005,2)` is false (verified); `100.010 = round(100.010,2)` is true (verified — trailing zeros are correctly tolerated because numeric equality is value equality).
2. **Typmod imposes a ceiling and errors on large values.** `999999999999.99::numeric(12,2)` → `ERROR 22003: numeric field overflow ... must round to an absolute value less than 10^10` (verified). That is literally a rejection for being large — a direct BR-21/SEC-R3/FR-BID-08/SC-57 violation. And the maximum declared precision is 1000 (`numeric(1001,2)` errors, verified), so even the largest possible typmod caps at 10^998.

The one write path (the bid function, ADR-2) inserts `round(p_amount, 2)`, normalizing every stored value to scale exactly 2 (`round(100::numeric,2)::text` = '100.00', verified), so `::text` output is already display-shaped.
rationale:
1. **NFR-DAT-05 is satisfied by the type itself.** PostgreSQL `numeric` is exact decimal arithmetic — no binary-float representation error exists anywhere in storage or comparison. Verified contrast: `100.01::float8 - 100.00::float8` = `0.0100000000000051`; the same operation in `numeric` is exactly `0.01`. "Never floating point" becomes a property of the schema, not a discipline.

2. **BR-21/SEC-R3 force P to be unbounded within this family.** Any finite P is a ceiling; the PRD's governance is explicit that choosing one is prohibited, not merely discouraged: SD-05 ("No implementer may introduce a price ceiling (BR-21)"), FR-BID-08, FR-CREATE-07, and PRD §9.2's accepted-consequence note ("Implementers must not add a maximum on their own initiative"). ADR-8 in ARCHITECTURE §20 says the same. Unconstrained `numeric` is the only variant of the fixed-scale approach an implementer is *allowed* to ship. It also beats the main rival (bigint cents), whose 2^63 limit (~9.2×10^16 halalas ≈ 92 quadrillion SAR) is a designer-chosen ceiling that overflows with an error — the same BR-21 violation in different clothes.

3. **Two-decimal discipline moves to a CHECK that rejects rather than rounds** — matching EC-06's required behavior and keeping ARCH §13.5's "Malformed amount" reason meaningful. The Tier-2 CHECK (ARCH §7) is the structural backstop; the Tier-3 bid function performs the same test first so the user gets the product-level reason (BR-27) instead of a constraint error.

4. **The comparisons the requirements are written in are native SQL.** BR-28's two branches are literally `>=` and `>` on numeric — no scaling, no epsilon, no conversion layer. Exact bid-function expressions (inside the SECURITY DEFINER operation, after `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and re-read per ARCH §13.2 steps 2–3):

```sql
-- step 6: well-formedness (BR-21 — scale and sign only; NO magnitude test)
IF p_amount IS NULL OR p_amount <= 0 OR p_amount <> round(p_amount, 2) THEN
  RETURN reject('malformed_amount');                                   -- §13.5 reason 5
END IF;
-- step 7: minimum acceptable bid (BR-28)
IF NOT v_has_bids THEN
  IF p_amount >= v_auction.starting_price THEN v_ok := true;           -- BR-29 INCLUSIVE
  ELSE RETURN reject('below_starting_price', v_auction.starting_price); -- §13.5 reason 6
  END IF;
ELSE
  IF p_amount > v_auction.current_price THEN v_ok := true;             -- BR-03 STRICT
  ELSIF p_seen_min IS NOT NULL AND p_amount >= p_seen_min THEN
    RETURN reject('outbid_by_concurrent_bid', v_auction.current_price); -- §13.5 reason 8 (EC-01)
  ELSE RETURN reject('not_above_current_price', v_auction.current_price); -- §13.5 reason 7
  END IF;
END IF;
-- steps 8–9: inseparable writes (BR-07, BR-13, SC-40, NFR-DAT-01)
INSERT INTO bids (auction_id, bidder_id, amount)
  VALUES (p_auction_id, auth.uid(), round(p_amount, 2));
UPDATE auctions SET current_price = round(p_amount, 2) WHERE id = p_auction_id;
```

(`p_seen_min` is the minimum the client displayed — informational only, never authority (BR-08); it exists solely to distinguish §13.5's race-loss reason from a plain too-low bid.) Deliberately absent per ARCH §13.2a: no maximum check (BR-21/SEC-R3), no increment check (BR-32), no leading-bidder check (BR-24/FR-BID-04), no reserve check (BR-35). Note there is no numeric expression in this function that could even *express* those checks — the type imposes no magnitude to test against, which is the strongest possible compliance with §13.2a.

5. **One representation for all three developers (S0-12, gap G-1, ARCH §19.2, §21.2):** Mohammed's `starting_price`, Rayan's `amount` and `current_price` are the same type with the same constraints, and the same `::text` string feeds the one shared formatter (NFR-DAT-08). No developer can invent a second representation because the schema only has one.
comparisonSemantics:
`numeric` comparison is exact value comparison, scale-insensitive, at any magnitude:

- `100::numeric = 100.00::numeric` → true (verified). SC-55's inclusive `>=` therefore holds regardless of whether the stored starting price has scale 0 or 2, and BR-12's "one bid per price level" cannot be defeated by scale games (100 vs 100.0 vs 100.00 are the same price level).
- `p_amount >= starting_price` (first bid, BR-28/BR-29, INCLUSIVE) and `p_amount > current_price` (subsequent, BR-28/BR-03, STRICT) are the entire amount rule — ARCH §13.2a: "anything else is not a rule of this product."
- A 0.01 delta is detected exactly at every magnitude: verified `10^131071 + 0.01 > 10^131071` → true, and `repeat('9',50)::numeric + 0.01 > repeat('9',50)::numeric` → true. No epsilon, no tolerance, ever — NFR-DAT-05's "precision must not degrade at scale" holds all the way to the format limit.
- Strictly-increasing history (NFR-DAT-03, FR-BID-15) follows mechanically: the threshold only moves up inside the row lock, and `>` is exact.

Pitfalls — all at the boundaries, none inside the database:
1. **Any cast through `float8`/`real` reintroduces drift** (verified: 100.01−100.00 = 0.0100000000000051 in float8). No money expression, index, ORDER BY, or test assertion may cast to float. This is the NFR-DAT-05 violation most likely to be introduced casually.
2. **JavaScript is a float trap.** JSON.parse gives float64: exact only to 2^53 ≈ 9.007×10^15. A client-side pre-check (Tier 1, UX only per ARCH §13.6) may mispredict above that — harmless, since Tier 3 decides (BR-08) — but client *display* from a Number is a real NFR-DAT-05/NFR-DAT-08 failure. Money must cross the wire as strings (see risks).
3. **NULL:** `current_price` is NOT NULL from creation (ARCH §12.1 step 3 initializes it to the starting price), so the comparison branches never see NULL; `p_amount IS NULL` is caught as malformed before any comparison.
4. Never compare amounts as strings ("9" > "10" lexically) — comparisons live in SQL on `numeric`, full stop.
displayFormat:
One canonical format, produced by ONE shared formatter module that both Mohammed (listing, detail, creation input echo) and Rayan (bid control, history, results) import — the structural fulfillment of NFR-DAT-08 and TEAM's S0-12 money rule:

**`<integer part with comma grouping>.<exactly two decimals> SAR`** — always two decimals, always the SAR label (BR-33; the term "Demo Points" is prohibited), input to the formatter is the amount's **decimal string** (`amount::text` from the database, already scale-2 because the single write path normalizes with `round(x,2)` — verified `round(100,2)::text` = '100.00'), never a JS Number.

Worked examples:
- `100` stored → **`100.00 SAR`** (padding is the formatter's job even if a legacy row has scale 0)
- `100.5` → **`100.50 SAR`**
- `100.01` → **`100.01 SAR`**
- `1234567.89` → **`1,234,567.89 SAR`**
- `90071992547409934567.89` → **`90,071,992,547,409,934,567.89 SAR`** — exact. A Number-based formatter (`Intl.NumberFormat` fed a float) would render this as `90,071,992,547,409,930,000` or scientific notation, violating NFR-DAT-05 and SEC-R3; the formatter must group the digit string itself.

Same string everywhere: listing card, detail price, bid input hint ("Enter more than 250.00 SAR", FR-BID-10), history rows, rejection messages ("the current price is now 100.00 SAR", §13.5), and result views. The same amount never appears two ways (NFR-DAT-08). One note for the team: the unresolved Arabic-RTL question (PRD currently says English-only) does not change this design — a later switch to Arabic-Indic digits or RTL layout is an edit to this single formatter, which is precisely why NFR-DAT-08 demands there be only one.
risks: THE TYPMOD REFACTOR TRAP (highest risk): a well-meaning dev or AI assistant later 'tightens' `numeric` to `numeric(12,2)` as apparent hygiene. Verified consequences: 3-decimal inputs get silently ROUNDED (100.005→100.01) instead of rejected, killing EC-06/FR-BID-07 and §13.5 reason 5; and values ≥10^10 raise `numeric field overflow` — a rejection for size violating BR-21/SEC-R3/SC-57 and the SD-05 prohibition. This matches ARCH §23 risk 10 (re-adding a removed check) and needs an explicit code-review tripwire; with all three developers vibe-coding, a schema-lint or migration-review rule ('money columns are bare numeric') should be written down once for every session, not policed per dev.

THE COLUMN ALONE CANNOT DELIVER NFR-DAT-05 END-TO-END. Verified: `to_json(numeric)` keeps full precision, so PostgREST and Realtime emit an exact JSON number — but the browser's JSON.parse converts it to float64, exact only to 2^53 (≈9 quadrillion; cent-exactness dies around 90 trillion SAR). Since BR-21 makes such values legal, money must be SELECTed as text (`amount::text`, or a view/generated column), Realtime consumers must re-read via the text path rather than trusting the payload number (consistent with ARCH §14.5 — realtime is a projection; the authoritative read recovers correctness), and no client code may ever hold money in a Number. This is a team-wide convention the DDL cannot enforce — the approach's biggest honest weakness.

CHECK violations on the DIRECT insert path surface as raw SQLSTATE 23514 errors. Bids are immune (ADR-2/SEC-Z4–Z7: the function is the only path and validates first), but auction creation inserts `starting_price` directly under RLS — Mohammed's form must pre-validate and map any constraint error to the specific message (ARCH §12.4), or users see database noise (violating SEC-T3/NFR-USA-03).

A PHYSICAL CEILING STILL EXISTS: verified `power(10::numeric,131072)` → ERROR 22003 `value overflows numeric format`. A ~128 KB digit string is sendable over HTTP, so this error is reachable by a determined tester. It must be caught at the boundary and mapped to §13.5 reason 5 ('Malformed amount' — the value cannot be represented), never surfaced as 'too large'. BR-21 read as 'mathematically no maximum' is unsatisfiable on finite hardware; this must be documented as 'no PRODUCT-imposed ceiling' (see noMaximumAnalysis).

UNBOUNDED ACCEPTANCE IS A SMALL ABUSE SURFACE: a legal 100,000-digit bid becomes a ~100 KB row broadcast to every viewer (ARCH §14) and rendered in public history (FR-BID-22). EC-25 requires display without layout breakage — CSS containment/wrapping work — and an oversized Realtime payload may be dropped by the transport, degrading liveness (acceptable: BR-22/RT-R7 — correctness unaffected, refresh recovers). Rate limiting is the PRD's existing answer to abuse, not a ceiling.

MIXED STORED SCALE if normalization is skipped: the CHECK accepts `100` (scale 0) and `100.010` (value-equal to 100.01). Mitigated structurally for bids by `round(p_amount,2)` in the single write path (ADR-2), but starting_price arrives via direct insert — either normalize in the creation flow or accept that the formatter pads. The formatter padding rule must exist regardless.

PERFORMANCE: variable-width numeric is slower than fixed-width integers and makes larger index entries for huge values. At NFR-SCA-01→04 scale (100 auctions, 50 users, 10 bids/min) this is negligible — stated for honesty, not as a real concern.

ROUNDING MODE never matters *only because* nothing ever rounds a user value: the design rejects non-2dp input rather than rounding (round() in PostgreSQL is half-away-from-zero — verified indirectly via the typmod trap). Any future code path that rounds money instead of rejecting reintroduces drift and must fail review (NFR-DAT-05).
sc56Analysis:
Setup: auction with starting_price = 100.00, zero bids, Active. All steps inside the serialized bid operation (ARCH §13.2: FOR UPDATE lock → re-read inside the lock → evaluate → write both facts → commit).

**Bid 1 — 100, accepted (SC-55).** Lock acquired; re-read shows no bids → BR-29 inclusive branch: `100 >= 100.00` → TRUE. Numeric equality is scale-insensitive (verified: `100::numeric = 100.00::numeric` is true), so this holds whether the client sent '100', '100.0', or '100.00'. Well-formedness passed (`100 = round(100,2)`). Insert `round(100,2)` = 100.00; `current_price := 100.00` in the same transaction (BR-07/BR-13/SC-40). Commit; lock releases.

**Bid 2 — 100 again, rejected (SC-56 first half).** If concurrent, it queued on the row lock behind Bid 1 (BR-11 — the lock order IS the definitive order). Re-read INSIDE the lock now shows one bid → BR-03 strict branch: `100.00 > 100.00` → FALSE → rejected before any write; state entirely unchanged (BR-23). Reason selection per ARCH §13.5: the client had displayed 'Bidding starts at 100.00 SAR' (p_seen_min = 100.00, inclusive); the bid met what the user saw (`100 >= 100.00`) but fails now → reason 8, 'Someone bid before you — the current price is now 100.00 SAR' (FR-BID-13/EC-01), distinguishable from reason 7's plain too-low. Exactly one bid exists at price level 100.00 — BR-12 satisfied, and no scale representation of 100 could slip a second one in.

**Bid 3 — 100.01, accepted (SC-56 second half).** Lock; `100.01 > 100.00` → TRUE, exactly — the delta is exactly 0.01, no epsilon, no tolerance (verified this holds even at 131,072-digit magnitudes). No increment check exists to demand more than 0.01 (BR-32, ARCH §13.2a). Insert 100.01; current_price := 100.01. History now reads 100.00, 100.01 — strictly increasing (NFR-DAT-03, FR-BID-15).

**Why the type is what makes this trace safe:** in float64, 100.01 is not representable (verified in-database: `100.01::float8 - 100.00::float8` = 0.0100000000000051). SC-56 is a knife-edge test — equal must fail, +0.01 must pass — and float noise on either side of that edge produces wrong accept/reject decisions precisely at the boundary the PRD chose to test. Exact `numeric` makes the edge deterministic at 100 SAR and at 10^131071 SAR alike (SC-57).
noMaximumAnalysis:
Three ceilings to distinguish, all verified live on PostgreSQL 17.6:

1. **Declared `numeric(P,2)` — a designed-in ceiling, and therefore prohibited.** Hard limit 10^(P−2); exceeding it raises `22003 numeric field overflow` (verified at 10^10 for numeric(12,2)) — an error whose meaning is literally 'rejected for being large', the exact thing BR-21, SEC-R3, FR-BID-08 and SC-57 forbid. Maximum declared precision is 1000 (verified), so the best possible typmod still owns a ceiling at 10^998. Unreachable in practice — but it is a number a human chose, and SD-05 plus PRD §9.2's accepted-consequence note say choosing that number is a product decision that must be recorded in the PRD first. Within the fixed-scale family, BR-21 therefore forces P unbounded: this is not a judgment call, it is the only compliant variant.

2. **Unconstrained `numeric` — a physical capacity, not a product ceiling.** Verified: 10^131071 (a 131,072-digit amount) stores and compares cent-exactly (`+0.01` still detected); 10^131072 raises `22003 value overflows numeric format`. So yes, an implicit ceiling exists at ~10^131071 SAR — no finite machine can honor 'NEVER rejected for being large' literally, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. The defensible reading of BR-21, consistent with its rationale ('no product or business requirement justifies one'), is: no *product-imposed* maximum. The format limit is the representational capacity of the mandated exact-decimal type — the same category as the HTTP body limit or a full disk, not a rule about auctions. Handling: the boundary maps SQLSTATE 22003 to §13.5 reason 5 ('Malformed amount' — the value cannot be represented in the system's numeric format), never to a 'too large' message, and this is documented in the PRD's spirit rather than silently relied on. SC-57's 'very large amount' test passes with ~131,000 orders of magnitude of headroom; no realistic or even absurd simulated bid approaches the limit.

3. **The ceiling that will actually bite first is NOT in the database: float64 at 2^53.** Verified that Postgres emits full precision (`to_json` of a 20-digit-plus-cents numeric is exact); the loss happens when browser JSON.parse converts it to a double. Above ≈9.007×10^15 (roughly 90 trillion SAR at cent precision), a Number-carrying client displays wrong digits — an NFR-DAT-05 'displayed exactly' failure well below any database limit. Because BR-21 makes such values legal, string transport for money (amount::text, string-fed formatter) is a *requirement consequence* of BR-21, not gold-plating. Under this design, the effective behavior at very large values is: stored exactly, compared exactly, displayed exactly from the text path, and never rejected for size within the physical format — which is the strongest 'no maximum' any real system can offer.

fatalFlaws: Variant A (BIGINT) outright violates BR-21/SEC-R3/EC-25: SQLSTATE 22003 at 2^63-1 halalas (~9.2e16 SAR) is a rejection for size, and ARCH 13.5's eight-reason contract has no legal way to report it (undefined ninth reason or opaque error, violating BR-27). The proposal concedes this ('non-compliant BY TYPE') yet still presents A as one of two variants, listed first and labeled 'the classic' — for a team of three vibe coders this is an adoptable footgun. Compliance requires striking Variant A from the S0-12 decision entirely, not merely arguing against it.
verdict: ADOPT ONLY AS AMENDED VARIANT B, OR PREFER THE NUMERIC(.,2) SAR COMPETITOR. The proposal's server-side core is genuinely airtight: SC-55/SC-56 resolve to bit-exact integer comparisons (10000 >= 10000 accepted; 10000 > 10000 rejected; 100.01*100 = 10001 in exact NUMERIC with no float anywhere in the path), the two-branch BR-28 predicate matches ARCH 13.2a verbatim with none of the four forbidden checks, bare NUMERIC + trunc CHECK is the only minor-units form that survives BR-21 (its refusal of NUMERIC(38,0) as an implementer-invented ceiling is exactly right per the PRD's accepted-consequence note and SD-05), and because ADR-2 denies direct insert, every misuse failure mode corrupts display, never outcome. But four specific cracks: (1) Variant A is a conceded BR-21 violation still offered as an option — fatal as packaged; (2) a real bug in the recommended variant's own sketch: p_amount_sar * 100 yields numeric '10001.00' (scale preserved), the trunc CHECK passes it, bare NUMERIC stores it, ::TEXT emits '10001.00', and the prescribed BigInt formatter throws — sar_to_halalas must trunc()-normalize or the text-boundary contract breaks on the first bid; (3) the ARCH 13.5 race/too-low distinction fires only when the client volunteers p_seen_price_sar — distinguishability becomes client-cooperative, degraded for SC-43-style direct callers; (4) the 2^53 JSON display cliff (~9e13 SAR) arrives 100x sooner than the SAR-NUMERIC competitor, and the Realtime mitigation (untrusted payloads + text-view refetch) is pure discipline. Which is the decisive point: the catastrophic error class here is the silent 100x unit-mix that type-checks and 'works' on every display surface, every pre-check, every ad-hoc query, forever — and the RPC-in-SAR/storage-in-halalas asymmetry plus two conversion sites recreates the exact G-1 three-representations hazard ARCH 21.2 exists to prevent. The proposal itself states that without enforced money-module discipline it is worse than NUMERIC(.,2) SAR; per MEMORY and TEAM.md, all three developers are vibe coders. The mitigations (columns named *_halalas, one money module, branded types, CLAUDE.md rules constraining every Claude session at once) are the right shape for this team and are why developerErrorResistance is 5 and not 3 — but they are guardrails around a permanent hazard the competitor simply does not have, purchased for a margin the proposal honestly calls thin (structural two-decimal enforcement and unit-explicit names; BIGINT's speed is surrendered by the only compliant variant and is worthless at NFR-SCA-04's ten bids/minute anyway). Recommendation for S0-12: default to NUMERIC(.,2)-style SAR storage (bare NUMERIC + a two-decimal scale CHECK to preserve BR-21) with this proposal's genuinely excellent boundary rules ported over — single formatter, always-two-decimals '100.00 SAR', text-typed amounts at every read boundary including Realtime, string RPC args, one shared conversion/validation helper. If the team insists on halalas, adopt Variant B only, with: Variant A struck, trunc() scale normalization, one shared sar_to_halalas used by both create_auction and place_bid, and the CLAUDE.md money-module rules made mandatory in the same commit. Sources: /Users/ry7vv/Documents/Coding_Project/dllal/PRD.md (sections 8.6, 9, 17.5, SC-55/56/57, SEC-R3, EC-25), /Users/ry7vv/Documents/Coding_Project/dllal/ARCHITECTURE.md (sections 9, 11, 13, 13.2a, 13.5, 15, 21.2, ADR-2, ADR-8).

APPROVE WITH CONDITIONS. Every load-bearing claim was verified against a live PostgreSQL 17.10: the domain's NaN clause works exactly as argued (NaN passes >0 and =round(x,2), only VALUE<'Infinity' kills it); the SC-55/SC-56 boundary holds exactly including mixed scales (100>=100.00 accepts, 100.00>100.00 rejects, 100.01>100.00 accepts); round(a,2)::text renders 40-digit values in full with '.00' and no scientific notation; to_char really overflows to '###' so its ban is correct; NUMERIC(15,2) really rejects at 10^13, proving 'choosing a precision is choosing a ceiling' (BR-21/SEC-R3/SD-05 — this proposal is the only PG representation without a chosen ceiling, and its 10^131072 residual is honestly disclosed and unreachable by any real payload). §13.2a compliance is clean and stated inline where an AI assistant would see it; BR-33 is respected; the '100 SAR' vs '100.00 SAR' tension is flagged for S0-12 ratification rather than silently decided (NFR-DAT-08). Conditions before S0-12 closes: (1) the bid function's amount parameter MUST be text, cast to numeric inside BEGIN/EXCEPTION — the proposal's 'catch 22003 on the parameter cast' is unimplementable with a numeric parameter (PostgREST casts before the body runs), so 'abc' and overflow payloads would surface as raw PostgREST errors, breaking §13.5's 'Malformed amount' reason and leaking internals (SEC-T3); worse, a vibe coder hitting that dead end may improvise a client-side length cap, i.e. a ceiling. (2) The string-transport rule does not cover Tier 4: Realtime postgres_changes payloads carry raw numerics as full-precision JSON numbers that JSON.parse corrupts above ~9e15 — the live price update (FR-RT-01) must treat the event as a trigger to re-read via a text-returning read, and this must be written down. (3) Pin the rules 'money columns are sar_amount, never bare numeric', 'one formatter (format_sar), never amount::text', and 'override typegen numeric→string' in the shared Claude session instructions for all three developers simultaneously, plus a review checklist item — the domain makes violations greppable but not impossible, and every client-edge failure mode passes casual testing until SC-57's end-to-end large-value test. Weakest axis is developer error resistance (7.5): the DB-side representation is near-uncircumventable, but the JSON/JS edge is a minefield only discipline fences, and supabase-js's path of least resistance (typegen number, parseFloat) silently violates NFR-DAT-05 above 2^53. No binding requirement is violated; no fatal flaws.

fatalFlaws: NaN slips through every guard and permanently bricks an auction (verified live on PostgreSQL 17.10). The special numeric value 'NaN' passes BOTH proposed CHECK constraints: `NaN > 0` is TRUE (NaN sorts above all numerics in Postgres) and `NaN = round(NaN,2)` is TRUE (numeric NaN equals itself, unlike IEEE float). It ALSO passes the bid function's entire well-formedness gate `p_amount IS NULL OR p_amount <= 0 OR p_amount <> round(p_amount,2)` (all three FALSE), and passes step 7 because `NaN >= starting_price` and `NaN > current_price` are TRUE. So a bid of 'NaN' is ACCEPTED, written to current_price, and appended to history. Thereafter EVERY honest bid is rejected `not_above_current_price` because `anything > NaN` is FALSE — the auction is unwinnable and its recorded winner is the NaN bidder at a NaN final price. This directly breaks NFR-DAT-05 (current_price is not an exact two-decimal value), NFR-DAT-01 (price no longer derivable/exact), NFR-DAT-03 (history not strictly increasing / cannot progress), BR-12 (price level unbeatable), NFR-DAT-04 (winner = highest bid is a NaN non-value), and FR-BID-16/EC-06 (a malformed amount is accepted, not rejected). The proposal's central claim — that 'scale and sign only' well-formedness is sufficient and there is 'no numeric expression that could even express' a bad-value check — is false: it never once considers NaN.

+Infinity has the identical failure (verified). `'Infinity'::numeric > 0` and `Infinity = round(Infinity,2)` are both TRUE, so it passes both CHECKs and the bid gate; `place_bid(3,'Infinity')` returns ACCEPT, current_price becomes Infinity, and a subsequent 80-digit honest bid is rejected. PostgreSQL's numeric input function accepts 'NaN','inf','Infinity' case-insensitively and whitespace-tolerantly, and PostgREST/Supabase RPC coerces a JSON string argument (e.g. {"p_amount":"NaN"}) straight into the numeric parameter — so this is reachable by a hostile client with a valid session, exactly the SC-43 / SEC-Z4 threat model. The direct auction-creation insert path is also exposed: `INSERT INTO auctions VALUES (2,'NaN','NaN')` succeeds, so the CHECK the proposal advertises as its Tier-2 structural backstop does not stop it. Only -Infinity is incidentally blocked (by `x > 0`). The design admits +Infinity and NaN into money storage and comparison; a bounded `numeric(P,2)` would have shared this hole, so removing the typmod bought nothing here while the proposal spent its whole risk section on float/typmod/physical-ceiling traps and missed the one value class that actually breaks correctness.
verdict: REJECT as written — do not ship without an is-finite / non-NaN guard. On its stated goals the proposal is strong: unbounded `numeric` genuinely honours BR-21 (no product ceiling), the SC-56 0.01 boundary holds exactly (100 accepted / 100 rejected / 100.01 accepted, verified), exact-decimal-never-float is the correct type choice, and the single ::text-fed formatter is a sound NFR-DAT-08 answer. But it contains a fatal, verified hole: NaN and +Infinity pass every CHECK constraint AND the bid function's well-formedness test, get accepted, and permanently brick the auction (no finite bid can beat NaN/Infinity), breaking NFR-DAT-05, NFR-DAT-01/03/04, BR-12 and EC-06. The gate must add `AND p_amount = p_amount AND p_amount <> 'Infinity' AND p_amount <> '-Infinity'` (or a CHECK using a finiteness test), mapped to §13.5 reason 5 'malformed amount' — on BOTH the bid path and the auction-creation CHECKs. Weighting developerErrorResistance heavily (as instructed) is what sinks the score: the representation pushes a large amount of correctness into unenforceable team conventions the proposal itself lists — never cast to float, always transport money as ::text, never 'tighten' to numeric(P,2), normalize scale, pre-map SQLSTATE 23514/22003 — and even the expert author, after verifying a dozen edge cases live, missed NaN/Infinity entirely. Three vibe coders using AI assistants will not hold those conventions, and the most likely 'hygiene' refactor (numeric → numeric(12,2)) silently re-introduces a BR-21 ceiling. Fix the NaN/Infinity guard and add a schema-lint/CI tripwire (money columns are bare `numeric`; every money write goes through the one function; a test that asserts NaN/Infinity are rejected) before this is safe to build on.
